comments.author: @kdl0
comments.text: In the end I think it will be about demand by the end users. What is the end-user lacking in their life? Is it increased productivity and efficiency and growth in their pursuit of money? Or is it human connection? Mental stimulation? Something else? I don't think AI productivity does much to increase a state of fulfillment and contentment in the average person. As interesting and cool as I find some of the tech, it doesn't really make me happy. So it could be that one GPU per person or whatever is too high an estimate of the demand - not sure I have any way to know how that equate to equity share price. At some point if you have these super ambitious people using AI to increase their power and influence to an exponential degree, and we already see hints of that - some people just don't know when to stop their amassing of wealth - there will have to be some sort of confrontation between the majority, which doesn't really care that much about power and influence, and the few delusional boneheads who don't understand how their own brain works (but may eventually, not saying that they will forever be chasing the drug of power over others.. but I also am not saying that I trust them to rehabilitate themselves either). To people who think I'm way out in left field, I pose the question - what makes your desires and the priority you place on things more important and correct than mine? If we are all inherently equal and deserve the same pursuit of happiness, don't you run afoul of that if you are forever trying to gain power and influence over me? When you take a disproportionate share of the resources? And if you think still that it is okay, well at some point there is still going to be a confrontation. I think giving certain individuals too much power will be a mistake. These sorts of endeavors should be nationalized for the greater good.

comments.author: @policani
comments.text: According to Grok, "by 2035, the U.S. (population ~350 million) faces increased competition for energy and water due to a boom in AI startups and data centers, particularly in states like Virginia (home to 35% of U.S. data centers) and the water-stressed Southwest. Data centers could consume 6-9% of U.S. electricity (300-450 TWh annually) and 2-3% of water (500-700 billion liters), straining grids and resources in regions like California and Arizona. During heatwaves, when demand peaks at 50-60 GW in states like Texas, rolling blackouts affect millions, with 5-10% of households facing outages lasting hours. Water rationing hits Arizona and Nevada, where data centers compete with agriculture and urban needs, reducing household water allocations by 10-20% in drought years. Rising energy costs (up 20-30% from 2025) hit low-income households hardest, with 15 million households spending over 10% of income on electricity. Wealthier communities and corporations secure priority access via private solar farms or premium utility contracts, deepening inequality. However, innovations like energy-efficient AI chips (reducing power needs by 20-30%), liquid cooling (cutting water use by 50%), and federal investments in renewables (e.g., $370 billion from the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act) mitigate shortages in progressive states. Grid upgrades and policies like energy caps or water recycling mandates in California and Oregon help, but lagging infrastructure in states like Texas risks persistent disruptions."
